rationale: The active-oil trial outside Parkinson disease gives a favorable 4.22-point adjusted constipation difference for extra-virgin versus refined oil. MEDI-PD's whole-diet comparison is inconclusive, and the MED-PARK protocol has no reported bowel results or assigned oil grade. The weak favorable lean rests on the active comparison outside Parkinson disease.

A blinded healthy-volunteer comparison found no clear separation in sleep reports after brewed leaf tea. A quasi-experimental inhaled oil study reported favorable insomnia scores with design and denominator limits. The Grande-Terre study describes a bedtime leaf infusion as customary use and gives no insomnia change. The minced-herb comparison in Parkinson disease remains unresolved.

Two additional oral comparator trials measured standardized depression scales outside Parkinson disease. One used high-oleic oil of unverified refining grade. The other used sunflower and fish oil together. The inhalation trial gave both groups the same sunflower carrier. The evidence leaves the effect of isolated oral refined sunflower oil on Parkinson depressive symptoms unresolved.

Pumpkin oil trials measured resting pressure and reported inconsistent results. A prostate trial described dizziness with tamsulosin and recorded none in the oil group. The Karli registry specifies seated pressure, and its supplement has no clinical pressure estimates. A commercial-oil rat study measured tail-cuff pressure. Cold-pressed oil and Parkinson orthostatic lightheadedness remain unresolved.

The healthy-volunteer crossover compares bedtime dried parsley tea with passionflower and finds no clear difference in morning refreshment. It does not measure daytime sleepiness or include an inert comparator. Four focused Europe PMC expressions returned zero records. The dried-parsley Parkinson sleepiness comparison remains open.

The Khalid abstract confirms mania after adding celery root extract amid two other exposures. Hallucination modality and frequency remain unverified from the original. Two separate celery cases report thyroid symptoms, and one uses dried leaf powder. None measures Parkinson visual hallucination frequency under dried leaf exposure.

Controlled processed-ginger studies in other populations generally favor constipation symptom scores or frequency. The review supplement confirms that its ginger study measured constipation by patient VAS in multiple sclerosis. Parkinson mixed formulas give mixed results and a registered ginger study compares two extract doses. Fresh-grated ginger and Parkinson constipation remain unresolved.
